name: Terminalia chebula (haritaki), in guggul with triphala
short: Guggul alone (the mix's other herb): possible cause of rhabdomyolysis in a case report; lowered propranolol and diltiazem levels. Mix trial: rash in 2 (4.3%) vs 0 on placebo.
text: The page's product is guggul (Commiphora mukul) combined with triphala, an Ayurvedic mixture of Terminalia chebula, Terminalia bellirica and Phyllanthus emblica (amla), taken by mouth. In a 3-month randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of this combination in 90 healthy people with high cholesterol, in which adverse events were a secondary outcome, 2 participants taking it (4.3%) developed a hypersensitivity rash compared with none on placebo; the trial cannot show which ingredient was responsible. A 2010 systematic review of human studies of herbal medicines for high blood lipids reports that no significant adverse effects or deaths were seen except in studies with some products, among them guggul and Terminalia belerica, Terminalia chebula and Emblica officinalis; the abstract does not say what those adverse effects were. Triphala without guggul (a different combination): a systematic review of 12 randomised trials (749 patients) reported no serious adverse event associated with triphala during treatment. Terminalia chebula alone: in a 4-week randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in patients with chronic schizophrenia, no serious adverse effects were reported with black myrobalan (Terminalia chebula) capsules. Guggul alone (the other main ingredient of the page's product, not Terminalia): a case report describes rhabdomyolysis (severe muscle breakdown) with haemoglobin in the urine in a 55-year-old man after 2 weeks of a guggul extract, with all values returning to normal after he stopped it; the authors rate guggul as a possible cause. In an 8-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 103 healthy adults with high cholesterol, 6 of the 67 participants taking a standardised guggul extract alone by mouth, at a standard or a high dose, developed a hypersensitivity rash compared with none of the 36 on placebo, and the authors say the extract appeared to cause this skin reaction in some patients; LDL cholesterol rose by 4% to 5% with the extract while it fell by 5% with placebo. This guggul-alone finding is consistent with, but cannot prove, guggul as the source of the rash in the combination trial. Interactions (guggul): in a randomised crossover study in healthy men, a single dose of gugulipid, a guggul extract, significantly lowered peak blood levels and exposure of propranolol (10 men) and diltiazem (7 men), and the authors say this could reduce the effect of these medicines.
